section.title: Esther's Banquet and Haman's Gallows
section.sectionRationale: Esther risks the unsummoned approach, and the scepter is extended: she finds favor and lives. But instead of pleading at once, she invites the king and Haman to a banquet, and then to a second banquet the next day. The delay looks strange, yet it sets the timing for everything that follows. Haman leaves the first feast elated, only to see Mordecai unbowed at the gate, and his joy curdles into rage. Egged on by his wife and friends, he builds a towering gallows for Mordecai, the very instrument that will destroy him.
section.thesis: Grace grants Esther access and life, and a hidden providence rules even her delay; meanwhile a proud man, unable to enjoy all he has because of one unbowed Jew, prepares the snare that will catch himself.
section.frameNote: Three movements: Esther approaching and the scepter extended; the first banquet and a puzzling second invitation; and Haman's rage that raises a gallows for Mordecai.

verses.text: On the third day, Esther put on her royal robes and stood in the inner court of the palace across from the king’s quarters. The king was sitting on his royal throne in the royal courtroom, facing the entrance.

As soon as the king saw Queen Esther standing in the court, she found {{chen|favor}} in his sight. The king extended the gold scepter in his hand toward Esther, and she approached and touched the tip of the scepter.
“What is it, Queen Esther?” the king inquired. “What is your request? Even up to half the kingdom, it will be given to you.”
“If it pleases the king,” Esther replied, “may the king and Haman come today to the banquet I have prepared for the king.”
“Hurry,” commanded the king, “and bring Haman, so we can do as Esther has requested.” So the king and Haman went to the banquet that Esther had prepared.

units.label: The banquet and a second invitation

verses.text: And as they drank their wine, the king said to Esther, “What is your petition? It will be given to you. What is your request? Even up to half the kingdom, it will be fulfilled.”
Esther replied, “This is my petition and my request:

If I have found favor in the sight of the king, and if it pleases the king to grant my petition and fulfill my request, may the king and Haman come tomorrow to the banquet I will prepare for them. Then I will answer the king’s question.”

units.label: Haman's rage and the gallows
units.note: the snare he builds for himself

verses.text: That day Haman went out full of joy and glad of heart. At the king’s gate, however, he saw Mordecai, who did not rise or tremble in fear at his presence. And Haman was filled with {{chemah|rage}} toward Mordecai.
Nevertheless, Haman restrained himself and went home. And calling for his friends and his wife Zeresh,
Haman recounted to them his glorious wealth, his many sons, and all the ways the king had honored and promoted him over the other officials and servants.
“What is more,” Haman added, “Queen Esther invited no one but me to join the king at the banquet she prepared, and I am invited back tomorrow along with the king.
Yet none of this satisfies me as long as I see Mordecai the Jew sitting at the king’s gate.”

His wife Zeresh and all his friends told him, “Have them build a {{ets|gallows}} fifty cubits high, and ask the king in the morning to have Mordecai hanged on it. Then go to the banquet with the king and enjoy yourself.” The advice pleased Haman, and he had the gallows constructed.

chen.gloss: Favor, grace, the unearned goodwill of a superior. Esther finding favor is a refrain of the book, first with the harem keeper, then the king, and now at the moment of mortal risk. It is the quiet vocabulary of grace: undeserved acceptance that grants access and life, a small window onto the greater favor God shows His people.

chemah.gloss: Hot anger, wrath, burning rage. Haman is filled with chemah at the sight of one unbowed Jew, and the same word describes the king's fury later in the book. Here it exposes the emptiness of pride: a man with everything is poisoned by a single slight, and his rage drives him to build the very gallows that will hang him.

ets.gloss: A tree, wood, or wooden pole; here the gallows, an impaling stake or beam some seventy five feet high. Haman raises it for Mordecai, but by the book's grim justice he will die on it himself. Scripture's pattern is that the wicked fall into the pit they dig, and the enemy's instrument of death becomes his own undoing.

basic.context: Esther steps into the inner court, and the king, pleased at the sight of her, extends the golden scepter: she is welcomed, and she lives. He offers her anything, up to half the kingdom. But rather than plead on the spot, she invites him and Haman to a banquet, and then, at the banquet, to a second banquet the next day. Haman goes home thrilled at the honor, until he passes Mordecai, who still will not bow. His delight sours into rage. He brags to his wife and friends about all his wealth and status, then admits it means nothing while Mordecai lives. So they urge him to build a huge gallows and ask the king to hang Mordecai on it in the morning. Delighted, Haman builds it.
basic.hermeneutics: The chapter raises two questions. First, why does Esther delay? The narrator does not say, but the pause turns out to be perfectly timed, leaving room for the sleepless night and reversal to come. Second, what does Haman teach us? He is a study in pride: he has everything and enjoys none of it because of one man's refusal to bow. The abiding lessons are the providence that governs even a delay and the self-destroying nature of pride, which builds its own gallows.
basic.originalLanguages: Esther finds favor, chen, the book's recurring word for unearned goodwill; grace grants her access and life. Haman is filled with rage, chemah, burning anger that a single slight kindles in a man who has everything. And the advice is to build a gallows, an ets, a wooden pole; unknown to Haman, it is his own death he is raising. The words quietly announce grace, the emptiness of pride, and the coming reversal.
basic.typology: The gallows Haman builds for the righteous Mordecai, and on which he himself will die, is a pattern that reaches its climax at the cross. There the enemy raised an instrument of death for the Righteous One and was himself disarmed and defeated by it. Esther clothed in royalty, welcomed by the scepter of grace, pictures the believer clothed in Christ and granted bold access to the King.
basic.christ: Haman prepares a gallows to destroy the man who would not bow, and ends up destroyed by it. This is the shape of the gospel: the powers of evil raised a cross to destroy the sinless Son of God, and through that very death He disarmed and triumphed over them. The scepter extended to Esther, granting her life and a hearing, pictures the grace by which sinners are welcomed into the presence of the King through Christ.
basic.god: God is not named, and yet He is clearly at work. Esther's favor, her strange delay, the timing that will soon expose Haman, all of it moves toward rescue under a hand the narrator never mentions. Meanwhile Haman shows what a life without God looks like: endlessly craving honor, never satisfied, undone by pride. The chapter teaches that God rules the timing of deliverance and that pride carries the seed of its own ruin.
basic.crossReferences: Proverbs 16 warns that pride goes before destruction. Psalm 7 describes the wicked man falling into the pit he has dug. Proverbs 11 says the righteous is delivered from trouble and the wicked takes his place. And Colossians 2 shows the cross turning the enemy's weapon into his defeat.
basic.oneStory: Grace welcomes Esther and a hidden God rules even her delay, while a proud man, unsatisfied by all his honors, builds the gallows that will hang him. It is a small picture of the great reversal at the heart of the Bible: the instrument meant to destroy the righteous becomes the undoing of the enemy, fulfilled when Christ conquered through the cross.

context.literary:
Chapter 5 is the first of a pair of banquets that frame the book's reversal, and it is built on doubling. Esther gives two banquets, the king asks twice what she wants, and twice he offers up to half the kingdom, verses 3 and 6. Haman leaves the court twice, once glowing and once seething, and two counsellors, his wife and his friends, give him one piece of advice. The doubled structure builds suspense in the way a folk tale does. The reader is told what the request is not, and must wait for what it is.

The chapter has an ABA pattern of moods. It opens with Esther standing alone in the inner court, a scene of fear that resolves into welcome, verses 1 and 2. It moves into a warm, wine-lit room where three people are at ease, verses 3 to 8. Then it swings to Haman's house, where a man with everything talks himself into murder, verses 9 to 14. The camera keeps cutting between two dinners, the queen's and Haman's, and between two kinds of speech: Esther's careful courtesy, 'if it pleases the king', and Haman's boasting.

The chapter's one list of Haman's glories, wealth, sons and rank, is in verse 11, and the narrator lets him read the list aloud and then confess that it counts for nothing. The chapter ends on a dark irony: 'The advice pleased Haman', verse 14, the same verb the narrator uses of the king's pleasure elsewhere. Haman is pleased to build his own execution platform. The tone is comic and terrible at the same time, and the chapter never lets the reader forget the danger, since the gallows is actually built.
context.historical:
The inner court of the palace at Susa was where the king sat on his throne facing the entrance to the hall, so that anyone who stepped in was seen at once, verse 1. Esther has waited three days, and dresses for the moment in royal robes. She chooses her own dress for a purpose, where earlier she took only what she was given. The gold sceptre, stretched out and touched, was the visible sign of the king's favour, and the ritual of touching the tip of it is the kind of court ceremony that shows how strictly access was ordered.

The phrase 'up to half the kingdom' is a formula of extravagant royal generosity. It is a courtly figure, not a literal offer, and another ruler uses it in Mark 6:23. Both kings are speaking in the style of a court where a wish could be spoken large, and where a sensible person would ask for something modest. Esther does not ask for anything yet, and that itself is a form of tact, since a wise courtier did not make her petition while the king's mind was elsewhere.

Persian banquets were also the setting for politics. Guests reclined, wine flowed and the king's mood was carefully managed. To be the only guest invited alongside the king would have been a signal honour to Haman, and Haman treats it as such, verse 12. The gallows, fifty cubits high, would have stood about twenty two metres above the ground, taller than a house and visible across the city. Persian rulers are known to have used impalement as a public punishment for rebels, and a tall stake or post made the point of a public spectacle. Haman's project is not just an execution; it is a monument to his own hatred.
context.canonical:
The chapter opens the second half of a pattern the Bible repeats: the arrogant person prepares a trap that catches him. The Psalms say it plainly. 'He has dug a hole and hollowed it out; he has fallen into a pit of his own making', Psalm 7:15, and 'the nations have fallen into a pit of their making', Psalm 9:15. Proverbs adds that whoever digs a pit will fall into it, Proverbs 26:27. Haman's gallows is a Psalm made into a narrative. Even the fear of man appears in the wisdom books: 'The fear of man is a snare', Proverbs 29:25. Haman is snared by the very honour he craves.

The theme of Haman's discontent recalls Ahab and Naboth's vineyard, where a king with everything sickens at the one thing he does not have, 1 Kings 21:4. It also echoes the tenth commandment, Exodus 20:17, and Jesus' warning that a life does not consist in the abundance of possessions, Luke 12:15. Haman's boast to his family, 'none of this satisfies me', is the reverse of Paul's word that godliness with contentment is great gain, 1 Timothy 6:6.

Esther's approach to the throne is echoed in the New Testament, where the shape is reversed. In Hebrews the believer comes near the throne with confidence, not with fear of death, Hebrews 4:16. The gold sceptre that gave Esther her life stands as a small type of the greater gift, 'the throne of grace'. In the same way, Esther's patient timing recalls the way God's purposes in Scripture mature slowly, as when a whole night passes before the dawn, Psalm 30:5, and the Book of Esther makes room for that waiting.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
The author wants the reader to see two kinds of power side by side. One is the power of a woman who approaches a throne with no authority except the favour she may or may not find. The other is the power of a man who holds a ring, a title and the ear of the king, and is still eaten alive by one man's refusal to bow. The story puts the two together to ask which of them is actually free.

He also wants the reader to be patient with Esther. The chapter does not explain her delay and does not apologise for it. It trusts the reader to learn, one chapter later, that the delay was the right length. That is a lesson about how people of faith often act: they take the next careful step without knowing the whole plan, and only later see that the timing was better than they knew. The author writes for a people used to waiting, and he offers no easy comfort but a story in which waiting is not wasted.

And he wants Haman to be recognisable. Everyone has met someone who is given a great deal and yet lets one small slight ruin it. The narrator's point is not that pride is wicked in the abstract but that it is self-consuming, and that it takes the counsel of friends who tell it what it wants to hear.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The chapter reports what Esther did and what Haman's household advised; it approves neither as a pattern to copy. Esther's plan of a double banquet is described without comment. It is not a recommendation to delay hard conversations or to manage people with hospitality, and nothing in the text presents her method as a general strategy. Zeresh and the friends give bad advice, and the narrator records it without endorsement.

What the chapter does teach by example is the danger of the friends who flatter. Haman had a chance at this point to accept the honour he had and let one slight go. Instead, he asked for counsel from the people who would say what he wanted to hear. A believer can hear a warning in that, to seek advisers who will say something hard. It also teaches by contrast: Esther asks others to pray and fast before she acts, and Haman takes counsel from those who share his anger. Which company we lean on tends to decide which way we go.

debates.question: Why does Esther delay her request to a second banquet?

views.label: A shrewd strategy
views.case: Some see a plan. By inviting Haman to a private banquet with the king, Esther builds the king's trust, isolates Haman from the crowd and prepares the ground to accuse him in front of both. The extra day also gives the king a moment to feel the honour of being asked, and gives Esther time to gauge his mood.

views.label: A failure of nerve
views.case: Others suggest that Esther loses her courage after the scepter is extended and puts off the moment. On this reading the second banquet is a further delay, and the story shows God using even her hesitation.

views.label: Providence shaping the timing
views.case: Many readers stress that whatever Esther intended, the delay sets up the sleepless night of chapter 6, in which the king reads of Mordecai's unrewarded loyalty. Whether by design or not, the extra day is exactly what the story needs. Proverbs says that a man's heart plans his course, but the LORD determines his steps, Proverbs 16:9.

debates.bearing: The text does not choose among these, and that may be its intention. Esther's motive stays hidden, while the outcome shows a wisdom greater than hers.

debates.question: Is Esther's conduct at the banquets a model or a warning?

views.label: A model of wise courage
views.case: Esther has just risked her life, fasted and asked others to stand with her, and her hospitality is the tactful continuation of that courage. She does not accuse in a burst of anger but uses the court's own customs to win a hearing. The Bible often commends people who act with wisdom and restraint, as when Daniel chose his words carefully before Arioch, Daniel 2:14.

views.label: An ambiguous and uneasy example
views.case: Other readers point out that she uses flattery and stages a trap, and that the book never says whether this is right. They argue that the book presents her cleverness as part of a world that is tangled and morally grey, and that its author does not turn it into a rule.

debates.bearing: Read alone, chapter 5 makes Esther look like a strategist, but in the wider story her wisdom is bound up with dependence on God shown in the fast. It is best treated as a description of a faithful person in a difficult court, and not as a template for how to handle every conflict.

study.originalLanguages:
Four small details in the Hebrew sharpen the chapter. The first is the phrase for how Esther finds favour in verse 2. The text says that she 'lifted' favour in his eyes, nasa chen, and the same phrase describes how she won all who saw her, Esther 2:15, and then the king himself, Esther 2:17. It is a phrase for grace received, not achieved. Esther 'lifts' what is given to her, and what she has been given comes again and again at moments when she is helpless. When the scepter is extended, the reader sees a pattern that started in the harem.

The second is the word for banquet, mishteh, which comes from the verb 'to drink'. It literally means a drinking feast, and it is the book's characteristic word for a royal occasion, used of Ahasuerus's feast in chapter 1 and of Esther's own in chapters 5 to 7. Esther's choice of this setting is an act of imagination. She takes the court's habit of wine and ease and turns it into a place of trial. Haman's own decree went out as the king and Haman sat down to drink, Esther 3:15, so the drinking table moves from the place where death was plotted to the place where it is undone.

The third is Haman's self control. He 'restrained himself', a reflexive verb that suggests holding oneself in, before he goes home and lets the anger out to his family, verse 10. The narrator is careful: the man who governs an empire cannot govern his own temper for more than a few minutes. The same restraint appears when Joseph holds back his tears before his brothers, Genesis 43:31. The difference is what is being held back, and why.

The fourth is the number 'fifty cubits'. A cubit was the length from elbow to fingertip, about forty five centimetres, so the gallows stood some twenty two metres high. The figure is deliberately excessive. Nothing but a spectacle needs such height. The word for 'wood', ets, is the same word that means 'tree', which will matter when the text is read in the light of Deuteronomy 21:22 and 23.

Taken together these details show a chapter built on contrasts of restraint and rage, grace and grasping, and a mishteh that becomes a trap.

typology.type: The gold scepter extended and touched
typology.fulfillment: Esther is welcomed on the strength of the king's favour and not her merit, and her life hangs on a hand held out. It is a small shadow of the gospel's welcome. Paul says believers 'have gained access by faith into this grace in which we stand', Romans 5:2, and Ephesians adds that in Christ 'we may enter God's presence with boldness and confidence', Ephesians 3:12. The escalation is that the welcome is now certain, secured by a finished sacrifice. The type falls short because a Persian king's favour was unpredictable and had to be won, while God's welcome to His people is settled in the cross.

typology.type: The gallows built for Mordecai and used on Haman
typology.fulfillment: The wood built to destroy the righteous becomes the means of the enemy's destruction. It is a pattern that the cross takes to its limit. The powers meant the cross as the end of Jesus, but God used it to disarm 'the powers and authorities', Colossians 2:15, and by His death to destroy the one who has power over death, Hebrews 2:14. The escalation is that Haman is caught on his own wood, whereas Christ willingly took the curse for others, Galatians 3:13. The type falls short because Haman was guilty and died for himself, while Christ was innocent and died for His people.

The snare that turns on its maker is a repeated pattern in Scripture: 'his trouble recoils on himself', Psalm 7:16, and 'let the wicked fall into their own nets', Psalm 141:10. It points to the deeper justice of God, who does not let evil have the last word. In Christ this justice takes a surprising form: at the cross the accuser is disarmed, and the 'accuser of our brothers has been thrown down', Revelation 12:10. The type falls short because it depicts a rough retributive symmetry, whereas the gospel offers mercy to enemies, Romans 5:10.

typology.type: Esther's banquet as a table where the enemy is exposed
typology.fulfillment: Esther prepares a table where the plot is revealed, and it recalls the Lord's word that He prepares a table for His people in the presence of their enemies, Psalm 23:5. In the new covenant the table is the Lord's Supper, where the death that broke the enemy's power is proclaimed, 1 Corinthians 11:26. The escalation is that Esther's table exposes Haman, while the Lord's table welcomes sinners. The type falls short because no human host can offer what Christ offers, His own body and blood for the forgiveness of sins.

study.christ:
Esther 5 leads to Christ through a pair of contrasts and one promise. It never names Him, and it does not need to, because the pattern of the chapter is one the New Testament takes up and completes.

The first contrast is access. Esther stands in a doorway that could mean death, and she lives only because a hand is held out. The reader is meant to feel how fragile such access is. The letter to the Hebrews sets that fragility against the confidence Christ gives, and tells believers to draw near 'with confidence' to the throne of grace, Hebrews 4:16. The believer does not wait for a sceptre to be extended. The way has been opened 'through the curtain of His body', Hebrews 10:20. Where Esther needed favour for herself, believers come in the favour of another. The gold sceptre is a picture of grace withheld unless given; the gospel is grace given before it is asked.

The second contrast is between two pieces of wood. Haman builds a tall post to display his enemy's death, and it becomes the means of his own. Jesus, too, is hung on a tree. Peter says that God raised Him 'whom you had killed by hanging Him on a tree', Acts 5:30, and Paul says that Christ became a curse for us, since 'cursed is everyone who is hung on a tree', Galatians 3:13, quoting Deuteronomy 21:23. Here the parallel turns into a contrast. Haman deserved the wood, and Christ did not. The powers that lifted Jesus up thought they were displaying Him as a criminal, and yet by that very act 'having disarmed the powers and authorities, He made a public spectacle of them', Colossians 2:15. The public shame Haman planned for Mordecai lands on Haman, and the public shame the world planned for Christ lands on the powers that planned it.

The promise is that the story will not end at the gallows. The proud fall and the humble are lifted, and this is not just a moral of the book but a pattern Jesus embodies: He 'humbled Himself and became obedient to death, even death on a cross. Therefore God exalted Him', Philippians 2:8 and 9. Mary's song says the same thing, that God 'has brought down rulers from their thrones, but has exalted the humble', Luke 1:52.

A caution belongs here. Esther is not Christ, and Haman's death is not the cross. The link is by pattern, not by allegory, and the details of the chapter, the sceptre or the banquet wine, are not codes. What the chapter does is prepare the mind to hear that the enemy's weapon can become the enemy's undoing, and that a small act of courageous trust may sit at the centre of a great deliverance.
study.god:
Esther 5 shows God without naming Him, and what it shows is worth listing carefully.

He is the giver of favour. Esther 'lifts' grace, and the text does not say why the king looks kindly on her. In a court where a moment's displeasure had ended Vashti's reign, Esther 1:19, a favourable glance is not a matter of course. The Bible ascribes such favour to God: 'the king's heart is a waterway in the hand of the LORD', Proverbs 21:1. Nothing in this chapter says He turned it, but the chapter is written to make a believing reader ask who did.

He is the God of timing. Esther's delay is not explained, yet it fits into a larger pattern that will come clear only in the next chapter. Scripture teaches that 'the lot is cast into the lap, but its every decision is from the LORD', Proverbs 16:33, and the book of Esther will soon show that the lots of Haman's own casting are overturned. Worship here means trusting a God who is not late even when the delay looks long.

He is the God who resists the proud. Haman is a picture of the person who has everything and enjoys nothing, and his fall begins in his own heart. James says that God 'opposes the proud, but gives grace to the humble', James 4:6, and Proverbs says that 'pride goes before destruction', Proverbs 16:18. The chapter shows that judgment is not always a bolt from heaven. It can be the working out of a heart that would not be satisfied, and in this chapter God does nothing visible at all. He lets a man build.

He holds justice and mercy together. The chapter shows both. Mercy comes to Esther in the scepter, and retribution is preparing in the gallows. The God who 'forgives iniquity, transgression and sin' also 'will by no means leave the guilty unpunished', Exodus 34:7. The book does not resolve this in one chapter, but it shows the two moving together, one for the people who are in peril and the other for the man who plots their death.

For worship, the chapter invites believers to bring their fear and their waiting to a God who is at work in the timing and in the favour they cannot explain, and to guard their own hearts against the poison of an unsatisfied ambition.

crossReferences.note: The king loves Esther more than all the other women, and she wins his favour and grace. Chapter 5 shows why that earlier verse mattered: the favour she has already received is what makes the scepter possible, and the story begins to pay off.

Haman sees that Mordecai will not bow, and is filled with rage, and decides to destroy all the Jews. Chapter 5 shows that the rage has not cooled. Even with wealth and rank, he cannot let one man's refusal pass.

Pride goes before destruction, and a haughty spirit before a fall. Haman's speech to his household in 5:11 to 13 is the proud spirit in action, and his fall follows in chapters 6 and 7 almost as a case study.

The wicked man digs a pit and falls into it, and his violence returns on his own head. The gallows Haman builds is the story's illustration of this psalm, and the psalm gives the reader the confidence that the story will end this way.

Whoever digs a pit will fall into it, and whoever rolls a stone will have it roll back on him. The proverb sums up the irony of Haman's project. In building a gallows for another, he prepares his own place.

Ahab sulks and will not eat because Naboth will not sell his vineyard. Like Haman, he has a kingdom and is undone by one refusal. Both stories show how discontent grows in a heart that has everything but the one thing it cannot have.

We are invited to come to the throne of grace with confidence to find mercy. Esther's uncertain walk to the throne and the sceptre held out for her make the invitation vivid, and show how much the way opened by Christ gives believers.

The LORD prepares a table in the presence of enemies. Esther's banquet, with Haman at the table and the king as host, is a human version of that picture, in which safety and hospitality are set in front of the one who means harm.

Anyone hung on a tree is under God's curse. The Hebrew word for the tree is the same as Haman's gallows, ets. The law explains why hanging was a public shame, and the reader who knows it will hear more in the story when Paul later applies it to Christ, Galatians 3:13.

study.oneStory:
Chapter 5 sits at the point in the Bible's story where the enemy's plan is at its most confident. The story began in a garden where a proud desire led to a fall, Genesis 3:5 and 6. It continued in the line of Cain and the builders of Babel, where the wish to be great without God led to violence and scattering, Genesis 4:8 and 11:4. In Esther, Haman is a late and vivid form of that impulse: he has been raised above every other prince, and he wants more. The snake in Eden said 'you will be like God'. Haman, who wants every knee to bow, has only a reflection of the same lie.

The chapter also answers an ancient question about justice. Where is God when the wicked seem to hold all the cards? Psalm 37 says that the wicked lie in wait for the righteous but that the LORD will not leave them in their power, Psalm 37:32 and 33. Esther 5 shows the wait. In the moment, the gallows is built and the righteous man still sits at the gate. The story teaches its readers to live in that gap. Faith is the confidence that the scaffold will do its work on the one who built it, even before anything visibly changes.

Looking forward, the chapter sets up the reversal of chapters 6 and 7 and the joy of chapters 8 and 9. In the larger Bible, that reversal is a repeated theme: the proud are brought down and the lowly raised, Luke 1:52, and it reaches its climax in the cross and the empty tomb. The cross is the biggest gallows in history, and it was the place where the powers thought they had finished the Righteous One. Yet God used it to disarm them, Colossians 2:15.

The story ends with the book of Revelation, where the great accuser is thrown down, Revelation 12:10, and the persecutors are judged, Revelation 19:2. There the pit dug for the saints is finally filled. Esther's scepter, held out in mercy, has become an open door, and the invitation to draw near is extended to all who will come. Haman's fear of being unsatisfied has no place in that city, where the redeemed are fully content in the presence of their King.

sermon.title: O Father, You Are Sovereign!
sermon.why: From Begg's series A Study in Esther, this message expounds Esther 5, Esther's courageous approach and delay set against Haman's pride and gallows, tracing the sovereignty of the unseen God over the whole scene. A faithful, expository handling of this movement.

quiz.q: What happened when Esther approached the king unsummoned?

options.text: She found favor, and the king extended the golden scepter, sparing her life.
options.note: Esther 5:2 shows the scepter extended, granting her welcome and safety.

options.text: The king had her arrested for breaking the law.
options.note: The law allowed death, but the king showed favor rather than punishment.

options.text: The king ignored her until she was summoned properly.
options.note: He welcomed her at once and offered up to half the kingdom.

options.text: She lost her nerve and fled the court.
options.note: She stood firm, was received, and made her invitation.

quiz.q: Instead of pleading immediately, what did Esther do?

options.text: She invited the king and Haman to a banquet, and then to a second banquet the next day.
options.note: Esther 5:4-8 records the delay that proves providentially timed.

options.text: She accused Haman openly in the throne room at once.
options.note: She waited for the banquets rather than accusing Haman immediately.

options.text: She asked the king for half the kingdom straight away.
options.note: The king offered that, but Esther's request was for the banquets.

options.text: She said nothing and returned to her quarters.
options.note: She acted, inviting the king and Haman to dine with her.

quiz.q: Why did Haman's joy turn to rage?

options.text: He saw Mordecai at the gate, who would not rise or tremble before him.
options.note: Esther 5:9 shows one unbowed Jew souring all of Haman's delight.

options.text: The king had insulted him at the banquet.
options.note: The banquet had honored Haman; his rage came from Mordecai's refusal.

options.text: Esther had refused to let him attend.
options.note: Esther had specially invited him; his fury was at Mordecai alone.

options.text: He had lost his wealth and position.
options.note: He still boasted of great wealth and honor; the issue was pride, not loss.

quiz.q: What does Haman's boasting and rage reveal about him?

options.text: The emptiness of pride: he had everything yet could enjoy none of it while one man would not bow.
options.note: Esther 5:11-13 exposes pride that no honor can satisfy.

options.text: That he was a humble man pushed too far.
options.note: The text shows arrogance, not humility; he paraded his status.

options.text: That he had genuine reason to fear for his life.
options.note: His problem was wounded pride, not real danger, at this point.

options.text: That he cared nothing for honor or status.
options.note: He cared intensely for honor, which is why one slight enraged him.

quiz.q: What did Haman build, and why is it significant?

options.text: A towering gallows for Mordecai, on which Haman himself would later be hanged.
options.note: Esther 5:14 sets up the reversal: the snare he built caught himself.

options.text: A monument to celebrate his own greatness.
options.note: He built a gallows for Mordecai, not a monument, and it became his own.

options.text: A prison to hold Mordecai indefinitely.
options.note: It was a gallows for execution, not a prison.

options.text: A gift to present to the king at the banquet.
options.note: It was an instrument of death for Mordecai, prepared in rage.

questions: Esther was welcomed by the extended scepter when she had every reason to fear rejection. How does it change your prayers to know you are welcomed into the King's presence through Christ?
Esther waited when she could have rushed, and her timing proved to be God's timing. Where is God asking you to be patient in a situation whose purpose you cannot yet see?
Haman had wealth, sons, and honor, yet one unbowed man robbed him of all joy. What small slight or ungranted thing is stealing your contentment right now?
Haman's pride drove him to build a gallows that would destroy him. Where might pride be quietly building something in your life that will one day fall on you?
The instrument Haman raised to kill became the means of his own death, a shadow of the cross. How does the reversal at Calvary give you hope when evil seems to be winning?

translationNotes.note: Put on her royal robes translates a phrase that literally reads she clothed herself in royalty, marking the dignity and risk of her approach to the throne.
Found favor, Hebrew chen, is a keyword of the book; the same grace that won Esther the throne now wins her a hearing at the moment of greatest danger.
The gallows fifty cubits high, roughly seventy five feet, is likely an impaling stake for public display; the height underscores both Haman's malice and the irony of his coming fall.
